assertions.description: Iterator.prototype.includes exists, so every iterator gets the method.
The basic contract: a value that is yielded is found.
A value that is never yielded returns false rather than undefined.
SameValueZero, not strict equality: NaN must be found. This is the semantic that makes it match Array.prototype.includes rather than indexOf.
SameValueZero also means +0 and -0 are the same value.
The method must stop pulling at the first match. Counting yields from an instrumented generator is the only way to prove laziness: a correct-but-eager implementation would return the same answer.
assertions.test: (()=>{let pulls=0;function* g(){for(let i=0;i<1000;i++){pulls++;yield i;}}const found=g().includes(3);return found===true&&pulls===4;})()

assertions.description: A generator that never returns must still answer, provided the value appears. This is the case that has no array equivalent at all.
It has to be usable at the end of a lazy chain, which is the point of adding it to the helper set rather than shipping a standalone function.

The iterator is left positioned after the match, so asking the same iterator twice gives a different answer. Surprising, correct, and worth pinning down: it is the difference between an iterator and a collection.
